title: Public, internal, confidential: how our data classification works

sections.title: Confidential and how to handle it

narration: Say your cursor is on Send.
going to a contractor who started this week.
beats.visual_intent: A monoline laptop screen with an email: an attachment icon labelled customer list, a cursor hovering over Send, then stopping.

grounding.claim: a customer list emailed to a new contractor

narration: Everything you handle has a class:
beats.visual_intent: The presenter speaks beside three outlined labels, each in its class colour, appearing as each class is named.

narration: Who could be harmed if it got out?
Not the file type, not the folder.
beats.visual_intent: A large question mark over a document outline; a file-type badge and a folder icon fade back as the narration says they do not decide.

grounding.claim: classes sorted by harm of disclosure
class decided by content and harm, not format or location

narration: It was approved for release, so anyone may read it.
beats.visual_intent: A monoline press release page gets an approved tick, its outline turns the public colour and it slides out to the open world.

grounding.claim: public means approved for release to anyone
public can be shared freely once approved

narration: Nothing alarming, but they are meant for colleagues.
beats.visual_intent: A meeting notes page sits beside the press release; its outline turns the internal colour as internal is said.

grounding.claim: internal is for employees, limited harm

narration: Harmless is not the same as approved.
Internal stays inside unless its release is approved.
beats.visual_intent: The internal notes move toward the outline of the building's door and stop at it; they stay inside.
beats.misconception: if it looks harmless it is fine to share outside

grounding.claim: public only once approved; harmless is not approval
internal not sent outside without approval

narration: If it got out, real people could be harmed.
beats.visual_intent: The opening customer list returns, rows of names drawn as lines; the harm question is applied and its outline turns the confidential colour.

grounding.claim: confidential: significant harm, need to know

narration: So it goes only to named people who need it,
It is stored with access limited,
and shredded or securely deleted when done.
beats.visual_intent: The confidential list travels one protected line to a single named recipient, rests in a locked folder outline, then a paper copy is shredded and a file deleted.

grounding.claim: only named people with need, via approved protected channels

beats.visual_intent: Three uncoloured outline items appear one by one above three empty trays in the class colours.

narration: but it stays internal unless its release was approved.
beats.visual_intent: Each item drops into its tray and takes the class colour; the org chart hovers over public, then settles in internal.
beats.misconception: org chart looks harmless so it is public

narration: The class travels with the information:
on paper, in a folder or on a screen.
beats.visual_intent: One confidential document turns from a printed page to a folder to a screen, its outline keeping the confidential colour throughout.

grounding.claim: label travels with information across formats

narration: Treat it as the higher class,
Our own policy decides each case.
beats.visual_intent: The rule large: an item with a dashed, uncertain outline steps up one class colour and an arrow points to an owner icon.

grounding.claim: when unsure treat as higher class and ask owner

narration: If so, use an approved, protected channel.
If unsure, ask the list's owner first.
beats.visual_intent: The opening email returns; the attachment's outline now shows the confidential colour, the cursor leaves Send and moves to a protected channel option.

grounding.claim: need to know and approved protected channel
